prompt: git merge printed CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in index.html. What has happened?

choices.text: The merge failed and nothing changed
choices.why: Something did change: Git merged what it could and wrote markers into index.html.

choices.text: It paused, waiting for a decision
choices.why: Right. Git merged what it could first. The merge is open until you resolve and commit, or abort.

choices.text: The repository is damaged
choices.why: Nothing is damaged. A conflict is a question, not a fault.

choices.text: Git kept main's version and discarded sunday's
choices.why: It kept both, between markers, because it refuses to choose.

prompt: Ana's branch changed menu.html and Bruno's changed style.css. Why did their merge need no decision?
hint: Git compares each side with the commit both grew from.

choices.text: Git always keeps the newer of two changes
choices.why: Git never decides by time. It takes both when they do not overlap.

choices.text: They were on different branches
choices.why: The Sunday conflict was on different branches too.

choices.text: No line was changed by both sides
choices.why: Right. Where only one side changed something, Git takes that side.

choices.text: Stylesheets never conflict with pages
choices.why: The files are irrelevant; changes to the same lines of any file conflict.

prompt: In a conflicted file, match each part to what it holds.
hint: You were on main and merged sunday.

pairs.right: The version on main, the branch you are on
The version on sunday, the branch merged in

right_distractors: The version from the commit both grew from

prompt: What happens if Ana runs git add and git commit without touching the markers?
hint: Git does not read the file for you.

choices.text: Git refuses while markers are in the file
choices.why: It does not check the content. add means settled, whatever the file says.

choices.text: Git keeps her side and drops the markers
choices.why: Git makes no choice at commit either.

choices.text: They are saved as ordinary text
choices.why: Right. The page would show them as text until somebody fixed it.

choices.text: The merge is aborted automatically
choices.why: Only --abort aborts. add and commit conclude it.

prompt: Put the steps of resolving a merge conflict in order.
items: Edit the file into the version you want, markers removed
git status says all conflicts are fixed
git commit to conclude the merge
trap: add before editing marks the conflict settled while the markers are still in the file.

prompt: In the middle of a merge, what does git add index.html tell Git?
hint: The status line changed after it.

choices.text: That the conflict in the file is settled
choices.why: Right. Status then says all conflicts are fixed.

choices.text: To start the merge again
choices.why: Nothing restarts. add moves the merge towards its commit.

choices.text: To keep the version in the staging area and discard the other
choices.why: It stages the file as it is on disk, the version you wrote.

choices.text: To track the file for the first time
choices.why: index.html was tracked long ago.

prompt: Bruno changed the opening time to half past six; Ana added Sunday hours to the same sentence. Which resolution does this section recommend?

choices.text: Keep Ana's line, since she is merging
choices.why: Being the one who merges does not make your side right. Bruno's change was deliberate too.

choices.text: Keep Bruno's line, since main is the main branch
choices.why: main is not more correct; it just happens to be where you are.

choices.text: A line with both: half past six, and Sundays from seven
choices.why: Right. Read both sides; often the answer keeps both.

choices.text: Abort, since conflicts mean the work was done wrong
choices.why: A conflict is two decisions about one thing, not a mistake.

prompt: What does git merge --abort do in the middle of a conflicted merge?

choices.text: Deletes the branch that was being merged
choices.why: The branch is untouched, ready to merge another day.

choices.text: Commits the merge with the markers left in
choices.why: --abort commits nothing.

choices.text: Returns all to the state before git merge
choices.why: Right. No markers, no half-finished merge, nothing lost.

choices.text: Keeps your side and finishes the merge
choices.why: That would be a resolution. --abort undoes the attempt instead.

prompt: Ana is on cheese and runs git rebase main. What does Git do?

choices.text: Moves main onto cheese
choices.why: main is not touched. The branch you are on is the one that moves.

choices.text: Makes cheese's commits again on top of main
choices.why: Right. Same changes, new commits, new ids.

choices.text: Creates a merge commit joining cheese and main
choices.why: That is merge. Rebase produces no merge commit.

choices.text: Deletes cheese and keeps its changes in main
choices.why: cheese still exists, on top of main now.

prompt: After the rebase, Charge 2.60 for cheese rolls went from 788a11d to 6e29a2d, with the same change and message. Why a new id?
hint: What else goes into the id?

choices.text: Rebase adds a marker to every commit it touches
choices.why: No marker is added. The id changed for a reason lesson 1 gave.

choices.text: Its parent is different now
choices.why: Right. The id covers the parent, and the new parent is 3a0003a.

choices.text: The date was set to the moment of the rebase
choices.why: The author date is kept. The parent is what changed.

choices.text: Ids are handed out again after a rebase
choices.why: Ids are never handed out; they are computed.

prompt: After rebasing cheese onto main, Ana switches to main and runs git merge cheese. What happens?
hint: cheese now starts where main ends.

choices.text: A fast-forward
choices.why: Right. main slides forward and no merge commit is made.

choices.text: A merge commit with two parents
choices.why: There is no fork to join any more.

choices.text: A conflict on every file cheese changed
choices.why: Any conflict was settled during the rebase.

choices.text: Nothing, since the rebase already changed main
choices.why: The rebase moved cheese, not main.

prompt: During a rebase, after resolving a conflict and adding the file: git rebase ___
hint: Not commit: the rebase has more commits to replay.

prompt: What is the one rule about rebase?
hint: It is the same rule as for reset.

choices.text: Always rebase before merging
choices.why: That is a team's choice, not a rule, and lesson 9 argues it.

choices.text: Never rebase main
choices.why: Close, but the rule is about who has the commits, on any branch.

choices.text: Never rebase commits somebody else already has
choices.why: Right. Their copy would hold the old commits and yours the new ones.

choices.text: Only rebase branches with one commit
choices.why: The number of commits is irrelevant.

prompt: Bruno already has 788a11d. Ana rebases it into 6e29a2d and shares her branch. What does the next exchange between their copies look like?

choices.text: Git spots that they are the same and keeps one
choices.why: Different ids are different commits to Git, whatever they contain.

choices.text: Bruno's copy updates itself to match
choices.why: Nothing updates itself; and his commit would still be there.

choices.text: The same change arrives twice
choices.why: Right. Two histories that disagree, which somebody then sorts out by hand.

choices.text: Ana's push is refused forever
choices.why: It can be forced, which is exactly how the duplicates arrive.

prompt: Match each statement to merge or rebase.

pairs.left: Keeps every existing commit and adds one
Replaces your commits with new ones
Safe on a branch other people already have

prompt: Which of these follow the practice this section describes? Choose all that apply.
hint: Rebase what is yours, merge what is shared.

choices.text: Rebasing your branch on main before you first share it
choices.why: Yes. Nobody else has those commits yet.

choices.text: Rebasing main onto your feature branch
choices.why: main is shared by everybody; rewriting it breaks the rule.

choices.text: Merging main into a branch that is already shared
choices.why: Yes. It adds a commit and rewrites nothing.

choices.text: Rebasing a colleague's branch you fetched
choices.why: They already have those commits.

prompt: Match each situation to the command.
hint: Two of them are ways back.

pairs.left: A merge stopped with a conflict you cannot deal with today
A rebase stopped at a conflict you have just resolved and added
A rebase went wrong and you want the branch as it was
Your unshared branch should start from today's main

prompt: Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of them is the belief that a conflict is a failure.

choices.text: A conflict means somebody made a mistake
choices.why: It means two people decided differently about one thing.

choices.text: Git commits whatever the file says after git add, markers included
choices.why: Yes. It never checks the content.

choices.text: A rebase can stop at a conflict on any commit it replays
choices.why: Yes. It replays them one at a time.

choices.text: After a rebase, merging the branch is a fast-forward
choices.why: Yes. It starts where the other branch ends.

choices.text: Merging more often produces more conflicts
choices.why: The reverse: branches that meet often have less time to change the same lines.
